explanations.explanation: Verse 2 says it plainly: “…the Lord delivered into his hand Jehoiakim king of Judah…” Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is the one who came to Jerusalem and besieged it (Daniel 1:1). Still, the text names the Lord as the One who delivered. It's a heavy verse, friend, so I'm not going to joke over it.

Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, really is part of Jehoiakim's story. He made Eliakim king and changed his name to Jehoiakim (2 Kings 23:34). So I see why his name came to mind. But Daniel 1:2 says the Lord delivered Jehoiakim into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.

Sennacherib was king of Assyria, and he attacked the fortified cities of Judah back in the days of King Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:13). That's a different invader with a different story. In Daniel 1:2 the Lord delivers Jehoiakim into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Sennacherib needs to stop crashing other kings' chapters, friend.

explanations.answer: To serve in the king's palace
explanations.explanation: Verse 4 says these young men are “…qualified to serve in the king’s palace…” Handsome, gifted and quick to understand, that's the résumé the king asks for. And remember, friend, he asks for all of it at once. Nobody gets to pick just one.

explanations.answer: To lead the army of Babylon
explanations.explanation: The verse never mentions an army. It says the young men are “…qualified to serve in the king’s palace…” Picture asking for someone gifted in wisdom and knowledge and then handing him a sword and a battle map. That's a different job posting, friend.

explanations.answer: To guard the treasury of his god
explanations.explanation: The treasury of his god shows up in verse 2, where Nebuchadnezzar puts the articles from the house of God. Verse 4 doesn't say anything about the young men guarding it. It says they are “…qualified to serve in the king’s palace…” Different building, friend, and different job.

Verse 4 says Ashpenaz is to teach them “…the language and literature of the Chaldeans.” Language comes first, which makes sense when you're going to work in a foreign palace. Showing up and not understanding a word anybody says would make for a long first week. I've had days like that in a junk drawer, and nobody was even talking.

Laws are a reasonable guess for a palace job, friend. But verse 4 says Ashpenaz is to teach them “…the language and literature of the Chaldeans.” Laws never make the list. Ask me to bake a cake from a cookie recipe and I'd give you the same look. The blank is waiting on a different word.

History sounds like a smart subject, friend. But verse 4 says the teaching is “…the language and literature of the Chaldeans.” History never gets a seat in that line. Pick it for the blank and the verse just politely slides it back across the counter.

Verse 5 says “They were to be trained for three years, after which they were to enter the king’s service.” Three years is a long time to be in training. That's more than a few batches of cookies, friend. The king was not rushing this.

This one is true, and the text gives the number. Verse 5 says “They were to be trained for three years, after which they were to enter the king’s service.” So the training does happen, and it lasts three years. Quite the long apprenticeship, friend.

Verse 7 says the chief official gave them new names. Daniel became Belteshazzar, Hananiah became Shadrach, Mishael became Meshach and Azariah became Abednego. Four young men and four brand new names in one verse. I'd need a minute just to learn how to sign them.

Robes are a fun guess, friend, but this passage never mentions them. Verse 7 says the chief official gave them names: Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. Nobody in that verse is getting measured for anything. I'd say the new robes are only in your imagination, and that's a good spot for them.

Verse 7 doesn't say anything about new homes. It says the chief official gave them new names. Daniel became Belteshazzar, Hananiah became Shadrach, Mishael became Meshach and Azariah became Abednego. The text gives us four names and no new addresses.

That's not how it goes, friend. Verse 8 says Daniel “…asked the chief official for permission not to defile himself.” He doesn't march up to King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. He takes it to the chief official.

Right, he doesn't go straight to the king. Verse 8 says Daniel “…asked the chief official for permission not to defile himself.” He starts with the chief official. Walking up to the king himself would be a much louder move, friend.

The chief official says, “For why should he see your faces looking thinner than those of the other young men your age?” He's thinking about what the king will see when he looks at their faces. I think he's nervous, friend. Nobody wants to be the one explaining skinny faces to a king.

Verse 10 doesn't mention any list. The chief official says, “For why should he see your faces looking thinner than those of the other young men your age?” His worry is about how they look. The names are not the concern in this verse.

The chief official never brings up training in verse 10. He says, “For why should he see your faces looking thinner than those of the other young men your age?” It's about what the king sees when he looks at them. I think that's a lot of pressure for one pair of cheeks, friend.

The chief official says it straight: “You would endanger my head before the king!” He's not worried about a scolding, friend. He's talking about his own head. I think he really did not want this to go sideways.

That one is true, and the chief official says it himself. He tells Daniel, “You would endanger my head before the king!” So he does name his own head as the thing at risk. That's a serious thing to say, friend.

Daniel asks, “Let us be given only vegetables to eat and water to drink.” That's the whole menu he puts on the table, and he asks for just ten days of it. Picture that request landing at a king's table, friend. I'd have asked for a cookie on the side.

Close, friend, but bread never shows up in Daniel's request. He asks the steward for a ten-day test, and bread isn't on the list. Ten days with no bread on the table, and I'd have my mustache sneaking a cookie under my hat by day two.

Fruit and milk sounds like a lovely breakfast, friend, but it isn't what Daniel asks for. Neither one is part of his ten-day test. Ten days with nothing extra on the plate, and I'd last about ten minutes before my mustache went hunting for chocolate chips.

Daniel says, “…compare our appearances with those of the young men who are eating the royal food, and deal with your servants according to what you see.” Compare is the word he picks. He's not asking the steward to take his word for it. He lets the steward look and decide, and I admire that, friend.

Report sounds official, friend, but it's not Daniel's word. He says, “…compare our appearances with those of the young men who are eating the royal food…” He wants the steward to look at the two groups side by side. Nobody is writing a memo here.

Daniel isn't asking the steward to explain anything. He says, “…compare our appearances with those of the young men who are eating the royal food…” It's about what the steward can see with his own eyes. A face tells the story without any explaining, friend.

It goes the other way, friend. Verse 15 says that at the end of ten days, “…they looked healthier and better nourished than all the young men who were eating the king’s food.” Thinner is exactly what the chief official was afraid of in verse 10, and it doesn't happen. Vegetables and water had a good ten days.

Right, they don't look thinner. Verse 15 says “…they looked healthier and better nourished than all the young men who were eating the king’s food.” That's the opposite of what the chief official feared in verse 10. I bet that surprised somebody.

explanations.answer: He keeps giving them vegetables instead
explanations.explanation: Verse 16 says “…the steward continued to withhold their choice food and the wine they were to drink, and he gave them vegetables instead.” The test ended and the vegetables kept coming. When something works, friend, you don't touch it. I'd do the same with my best cookie recipe.

explanations.answer: He puts them back on the royal food
explanations.explanation: That's not what the steward does. Verse 16 says he “…continued to withhold their choice food and the wine they were to drink, and he gave them vegetables instead.” The four of them stay on vegetables. The royal food doesn't come back for them.

explanations.answer: He asks the king for ten more days
explanations.explanation: The text never has the steward going to the king for more days. Verse 16 says he “…continued to withhold their choice food and the wine they were to drink, and he gave them vegetables instead.” He just keeps the vegetables coming. Quiet and simple, friend.

explanations.answer: All kinds of visions and dreams
explanations.explanation: Verse 17 says, “And Daniel had insight into all kinds of visions and dreams.” The four got knowledge and understanding in every kind of literature and wisdom. Then Daniel gets this extra, friend. That's a gift on top of a gift.

Laws of Babylon are not in verse 17. It says, “And Daniel had insight into all kinds of visions and dreams.” That's the extra gift the text names for him. A law book would be a very different kind of gift, friend.

explanations.answer: All the stars in the sky
explanations.explanation: My own sky gets a new star for every finished cookie box, but that's my sky, friend. Daniel's gift in verse 17 is that he “…had insight into all kinds of visions and dreams.” The text says nothing about stars. Dreams and visions are his lane.

Verse 19 says the king spoke with them, “…and among all the young men he found no one equal to Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.” Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, looked at the whole group and found no one equal to these four. Then they entered the king's service. Three years of training, and these four came out on top.

That one is true, friend. Verse 19 says the king spoke with them, “…and among all the young men he found no one equal to Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.” Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, compares all of them and finds nobody who matches those four. So they enter the king's service.

explanations.answer: Ten times better than all of them
explanations.explanation: Verse 20 says the king “…found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his entire kingdom.” Ten times, friend, and not just better than the average one. That's better than all of them. Let that sit for a second.

explanations.answer: Just as wise as the best of them
explanations.explanation: The text says more than that, friend. Verse 20 says the king “…found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his entire kingdom.” That's not matching the best one, it's ten times better than all of them. Don't sell them short.

explanations.answer: Second only to the chief enchanter
explanations.explanation: Verse 20 doesn't mention a chief enchanter at all. It says the king “…found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his entire kingdom.” Nobody sits above them in that line. Not second place, friend, ten times better.
